# Feature selection and boosting

## Assignment submission

All R instruction files and presentations of the results are to be submitted in a `.zip` archive via the course messaging tool to **Rafael Pino** (`.RMarkdown` files are accepted).

**Deadline:** 10 May.

---

## Data description

We use the same *data frame* `datos` generated in the *Machine Learning I* assignment.

Recall that:

- It contains **1000 cases**.
- It includes the variable `label` (categorical, distinguishing two garment types).
- It contains **10 potentially predictive variables** for `label`.
- These variables correspond to the content of 10 pixels selected among the 784 greyscale pixels of each 28×28 image.

---

## Tasks

1. **Data partition**
   
   - Split the data into *train* and *test* subsets (75% and 25%).
   We replicate the partition used in the *Machine Learning I* assignment to ensure comparability of results.
```{r}
# First five digits of the national ID (seed)
m <- 29509
# Load data-generation script
source("data/GenerarDatos.R")

set.seed(12345)
m <- dim(datos)[1] # number of cases
test <- sample(1:m, size = 0.25 * m, replace = FALSE)
# training set
x_train <- datos[-test,]
# test set
x_test <- datos[test,]
```


2. **Feature selection and LDA**
   - Apply **two feature-selection techniques**.
We start with attribute-importance-based selection.
```{r}
pesos_1 = FSelector::cfs(label~.,datos)
pesos_1
```

We also try genetic-algorithm-based feature selection.
```{r}
set.seed(12345)
ga_control = gafsControl(functions = rfGA, method = "cv", number = 4)
pesos_2 = gafs(x = datos[, !(names(datos) %in% "label")], y = datos$label,
                  popSize=20, pcrossover=0.8, pmutation=0.1, iters = 3,
                  gafsControl = ga_control)
print(pesos_2)
```
We select the five most relevant variables highlighted by the function output, while noting that it actually selects eight ("In the final search using the entire training set:
   * 8 features selected at iteration 1 including:
     pixel81, pixel125, pixel161, pixel211, pixel640 ..")

   - With each selection, build a classification model based on **Fisher's linear discriminant analysis (LDA)**.
   
   First selection of variables:
```{r}
modeloADL_1 = lda(label ~ pixel125+pixel528+pixel733+pixel745, datos)
modeloADL_1
```
The discriminant direction formula is $$
LD1 =
-0.014629900\,x_{125}
+0.011556774\,x_{528}
-0.005678291\,x_{733}
-0.002634348\,x_{745}
$$
If the separating hyperplane equation is needed, it suffices to consider
$$LD1 + c = 0$$
where $c$ is the cut-off point.

Second selection of variables:
```{r}
modeloADL_2 = lda(label ~ pixel125, datos)
modeloADL_2
```

   - Evaluate and compare both models.
```{r}
plot(cumsum(100*modeloADL_1$svd^2/sum(modeloADL_1$svd^2) ),type="h",
     main="Cumulative separation capacity",
     xlab="Number of FLDs",
     ylab="% separation")
abline(h=90,col="red")
```
With a binary response we obtain a single separation, so this plot is not informative. We therefore study the confusion matrix and associated metrics.

```{r}
# =========================
# MODEL 1
# =========================
pred1 <- predict(modeloADL_1, newdata = x_test)$class

cm1 <- confusionMatrix(
  factor(pred1),
  factor(x_test$label),
  positive = "Ankle boot" 
)

cm1

# Extract metrics
metrics1 <- c(
  Accuracy  = cm1$overall["Accuracy"],
  Precision = cm1$byClass["Pos Pred Value"],
  Recall    = cm1$byClass["Sensitivity"],
  F1_Score  = cm1$byClass["F1"]
)

metrics1
```
For the first model we obtain about 90\% accuracy, together with a 95\% confidence interval for that accuracy. The no-information rate provides a baseline; the line P-Value [Acc > NIR] : < 2.2e-16 tests whether the model beats that baseline. The tiny p-value lets us reject the null and conclude that the model performs better.
```{r}
# =========================
# MODEL 2
# =========================
pred2 <- predict(modeloADL_2, newdata = x_test)$class

cm2 <- confusionMatrix(
  factor(pred2),
  factor(x_test$label),
  positive = "Ankle boot" 
)

cm2

# Extract metrics
metrics2 <- c(
  Accuracy  = cm2$overall["Accuracy"],
  Precision = cm2$byClass["Pos Pred Value"],
  Recall    = cm2$byClass["Sensitivity"],
  F1_Score  = cm2$byClass["F1"]
)

metrics2
```
```{r}
# =========================
# COMPARISON TABLE
# =========================
comparison <- rbind(
  Modelo_ADL_1 = metrics1,
  Modelo_ADL_2 = metrics2
)

comparison
```
Both models are strong (accuracy above 0.88). The first is clearly better, but also more complex because it uses five predictors. The key difference is the ability to predict the "Pullover" class: the second model, with a single predictor, misclassifies 26 cases, while the first does much better. This shows up in specificity and, of course, in precision.

3. **Gradient Boosting model**
   
   - Using the `train` function from the `caret` package, build and evaluate a **Gradient Boosting** model.
```{r}
train_control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

grid <- expand.grid(n.trees = c(100,250,500),
                    interaction.depth = c(1,3,5,7),
                    shrinkage = c(0.01, 0.1),
                    n.minobsinnode = 25)

tuned_modelo <- train(label ~ ., 
                     data = x_train, 
                     method = "gbm", verbose=FALSE, 
                     distribution="bernoulli",
                     trControl = train_control, 
                     tuneGrid = grid)
tuned_modelo
```
After the grid search the chosen model is n.trees = 250, interaction.depth = 7, shrinkage = 0.1 and n.minobsinnode = 25.
Performance metrics:

```{r}
pred <- predict(tuned_modelo, newdata = x_test)

cm <- confusionMatrix(
  factor(pred),
  factor(x_test$label),
  positive = "Pullover" 
)

cm

# Extract metrics
metrics <- c(
  Accuracy  = cm$overall["Accuracy"],
  Precision = cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"],
  Recall    = cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
  F1_Score  = cm$byClass["F1"]
)

metrics
```
This model outperforms the previous ones with strong metrics overall. McNemar's Test P-Value rejects the null of equal probability of misclassification in the first and second categories.
```{r}
probabi=predict(tuned_modelo, x_test,type="prob")[,1] #Prob. pos
prediobj<-prediction(probabi,x_test$label)
plot(performance(prediobj, "tpr","fpr"),
     main="ROC TEST. Gradient Boosting",
     xlab="False positive rate", 
     ylab="True positive rate")
abline(a=0,b=1,col="blue",lty=2)
auc<- as.numeric(performance(prediobj,"auc")@y.values)
legend("bottomright",legend=paste("AUC=",round(auc,3)))
```
The ROC curve and AUC also confirm that this is a good model.

4. **XGBoost model**
   - Build and evaluate an **XGBoost** model.
  We prepare the data and fit the model:
```{r}
y_factor <- as.factor(x_train$label)
table(y_factor)

y <- as.integer(y_factor)-1
table(y)

X_ent <- data.matrix(x_train[ , -which(names(x_train) == "label")])
dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = X_ent, label = y)

params <- list(
  objective = "binary:logistic",
  eval_metric = "logloss",
  max_depth = 4,
  learning_rate = 0.1,
  nthread = 2
)
```
```{r}
modelo_xgboost <- xgb.train(
  params = params,
  data = dtrain,
  nrounds = 10
)
```



   - Compare the results with the previous model.
```{r}
X_test <- data.matrix(x_test[, -which(names(x_test) == "label")])
dtest <- xgb.DMatrix(data = X_test)
y_test <- as.integer(as.factor(x_test$label))-1


pred_xgboost <- predict(modelo_xgboost, dtest)
pred_class <- ifelse(pred_xgboost > 0.5, 1, 0)
```

```{r}
mconf_xgboost <- table(Pred=pred_class,Real=y_test)
mconf_xgboost
```

```{r}
Acierto=round(100*sum(diag(prop.table(mconf_xgboost))),2)
SensEspec=round(100*diag(prop.table(mconf_xgboost,1)),2)
cat(" Test accuracy (%)= \t\t",
    Acierto,"%\n",
    "Test sensitivity (pos)= \t\t",
    SensEspec[2],"%\n",
    "Test specificity (neg)=  \t\t",
    SensEspec[1] ,"%\n")


probabix=predict(modelo_xgboost, dtest)
prediobjx<-prediction(probabix,y_test)
```
Overall we obtain worse results than the previous model on every metric. Preferring the Gradient Boosting model is more sensible.
   
```{r}
plot(performance(prediobjx, "tpr","fpr"),
     main="ROC TEST. XGBoost",
     xlab="False positive rate", 
     ylab="True positive rate")
abline(a=0,b=1,col="blue",lty=2)
auc<- performance(prediobjx,"auc")@y.values[[1]]
legend("bottomright",legend=paste("AUC=",round(auc,3)))
```
The AUC points to the same conclusion.
